blocks.x: Risk and forecasting models with signed baselines, time-based holdouts and governance that survives the quarter they are judged in: predictions built to be checked, not presentations built to be believed.
A forecast earns trust by being falsifiable

Predictive analytics fails quietly: the model was good in the notebook, decent at launch, and three quarters later nobody knows it drifted. We build risk and forecasting with the decision-domain's discipline — signed baselines, time-based holdouts, champion-challenger on live data — because a prediction that cannot be scored against reality is an opinion.
The practice spans credit and operational risk, demand and capacity forecasting, and early-warning systems — always with the governance layer that says who may act on the model and under what bounds.
Below: the failure modes that make analytics theater, the reference architecture that keeps models honest, and the console the risk function reads.
Four failure modes that make analytics theater
Every one of these produces beautiful numbers that collapse in the quarter they were meant to serve — the countermeasures make the model falsifiable and the action real.

blocks.x: Reference architecture — baselines, holdouts and the action loop

The architecture enforces humility structurally: every model ships beside its signed baseline, holdouts are time-based rather than random, leakage screens run on every feature set, and the action loop records what the prediction actually caused.
